articles.title: DeepSeek's Super-Agent Prototype: Router + Workers
articles.summary: An MIT-licensed research prototype showing a router agent decomposing work for small worker agents.
articles.problem: One agent doing everything in one context gets tangled on multi-step work. Conversation, task selection, execution, and follow-up compete for the same attention, so routine work can stall behind a single long task.
articles.solution: DeepSeek's MIT-licensed dsh-superagent-prototype separates those jobs. A long-running Router handles interaction and dispatch, while isolated Worker sessions execute individual work items and return results to the original conversation.
articles.benefit: The pattern gives parallel work cleaner boundaries: the router stays responsive, workers can be isolated by task, and results can be merged back without turning one session into a bottleneck.
articles.apply: Treat it as a design reference for our own hourly todo-check automation, not as production software. Borrow the router/worker split, narrow worker authority, and the rule that the system should speak only when a person must act or can use a result.

articles.title: Opportunity: Layout for Illustrated & Complex Books
articles.summary: Formatting tools handle plain prose; image-fixed books still need a human, at $600–$2,500 per book.
articles.problem: Authors of illustrated and complex-layout books have no affordable self-serve option. Their images, captions, sidebars, and page-specific compositions cannot simply reflow like ordinary prose.
articles.solution: Build a layout tool specifically for image-fixed interiors — picture books, cookbooks, manuals, and other designed pages — instead of adapting a prose formatter after the fact.
articles.benefit: Authors could get print-ready files at a fraction of the human price and turnaround, while the product focuses on a segment existing tools serve poorly.
articles.apply: Start with one narrow MVP: fixed-layout picture books, a small set of dependable page templates, and a clean print-ready export. Charge per book and expand to adjacent complex formats only after authors validate the first workflow.

articles.title: claude-mem: Persistent Memory for AI Coding Agents
articles.summary: An open-source system that gives coding agents a memory across sessions, so they stop starting from zero.
articles.problem: AI agents forget everything between sessions; re-briefing them burns time and tokens, and context is lost.
articles.solution: claude-mem (Apache 2.0) hooks the agent lifecycle, compresses what happened into observations stored in SQLite + FTS5 with vector search, and retrieves them with progressive disclosure: compact index first, then timeline, then full detail only for chosen items.
articles.benefit: Continuity without stuffing huge context into every session; cheaper, faster restarts.
articles.apply: Our team is running a scoped trial — storytelling repo only, offline opt-in, Gemini (free) as the compression provider, 3–5 sessions, then a fresh-session recall test; curated memory files stay the authority during the trial.

articles.title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: A Serious Local Agent Brain
articles.summary: Liquid AI's open-weight 24B mixture-of-experts model with only ~2.45B active parameters, aimed at agent work.
articles.problem: Local models have been too weak for real agent tasks, pushing teams to paid APIs.
articles.solution: LFM2.5-24B-A2B uses mixture-of-experts efficiency: a 24B model with only about 2.45B active parameters per token, post-trained for reasoning and tool use on local devices.
articles.benefit: It offers a plausible free local brain for PC-side agent roles, with big-model capacity at a much smaller active running cost. Its published benchmark results are Liquid AI's own, so they still need independent confirmation.
articles.apply: Use it first as a candidate for testbed roles on the team PC. Check real task quality against our current models, and read the LFM 1.0 license carefully before adoption because it has a $10M revenue condition.

articles.kicker: Cash flow without the awkward chase
articles.title: Opportunity: AI Invoice Chasing for Solo Freelancers
articles.summary: 64% of freelancers report late payments with ~$5,600 outstanding on average, while serious AR tools cost $49–$1,500+/month.
articles.problem: Solo freelancers lose cash flow and hours to awkward manual payment chasing. Enterprise accounts-receivable products are too expensive and heavy for a one-person business.
articles.solution: Layer AI-drafted, escalating reminder sequences — polite first, then progressively firmer — on top of the free invoicing tools freelancers already use.
articles.benefit: Freelancers can get paid on time without personally carrying the social cost of chasing clients, and without paying enterprise AR prices.
articles.apply: The smallest MVP connects an invoice list, generates the reminder sequence for approval, and sends it on schedule. Price it as a small monthly subscription positioned clearly under the $49–$1,500+/month enterprise tools.

articles.title: GitHub Agentic Workflows: Agents Inside GitHub Actions
articles.summary: Write a Markdown file and get an agent-powered GitHub Actions workflow (generally available Oct 28, 2026).
articles.problem: When a CI pipeline goes red, a human has to read logs and triage before anyone learns anything.
articles.solution: GitHub Agentic Workflows let an AI agent investigate a failure, gather evidence, and report as part of the pipeline itself. Teams define the automation in natural-language Markdown, which is compiled into standard GitHub Actions YAML.
articles.benefit: A broken build can get a faster first diagnosis without a person babysitting the run or manually collecting the first round of evidence.
articles.apply: The natural candidate for our deploy pipeline is an auto-investigation of failed “Deploy dev” runs, with findings posted back to the team. The default Copilot engine needs a paid license, so choose the workflow engine deliberately in a free-first setup.

articles.title: EmbeddingGemma 2: Open Embeddings for Local RAG
articles.summary: Google's open (Apache 2.0) multimodal embedding model, a candidate to power local search.
articles.problem: RAG quality stands or falls on the embedding model, and cloud embedding APIs cost money and add latency.
articles.solution: EmbeddingGemma 2 is a small open-weight embedder that can run locally and map different content types into a shared retrieval space.
articles.benefit: It could provide free, private, fast embeddings for our local RAG over team documents, keeping the corpus and queries on our own machine.
articles.apply: Do not switch on the announcement alone. A/B test EmbeddingGemma 2 against our current bge-small-en-v1.5 plus MiniLM reranker on the same corpus, compare retrieval quality and speed, and only then decide whether it earns the replacement.

articles.title: agent-token-saver: Cut Agent Token Spend With Hooks
articles.summary: MIT, stdlib-only hooks that trimmed 19.67% of provider tokens in a real Codex A/B run.
articles.problem: Agent sessions waste tokens on verbose, repeated tool output, oversized files, long logs, and broad skill or tool catalogs that are not needed for the current decision.
articles.solution: agent-token-saver uses small, standard-library hooks and bounded projections to strip or compress that noise before it reaches the model, while preserving the evidence needed for the task.
articles.benefit: In the project's real Codex A/B, provider-reported tokens fell 19.67% in aggregate — the same work for fewer tokens, aligned with our standing token-discipline goal.
articles.apply: Trial it on a non-critical workflow and measure before/after by task. One task in the A/B used 32.16% more tokens, so never assume a universal saving or roll it out without per-task evidence.
